story.title: A sentence can be fluent and still be the wrong translation
paragraphs: A document gives a sentence more than background information. Earlier mentions can determine which person a pronoun refers to; later sentences can reveal which sense of a word was intended. An evaluator that sees only the current source, translation, and reference must judge without evidence that a human reader already has. The paper starts from this mismatch between the information used to annotate quality and the information used to predict that annotation.

Yet expanding the input is not sufficient. A sentence-level metric has learned which tokens its quality score describes. Prepending a paragraph at inference changes that input distribution and can blur the distinction between a good surrounding passage and a bad target sentence. The central tension is therefore selective access plus training: provide enough document evidence to interpret the target, while keeping the judgment focused on that target.

mechanism.title: Context changes the representation; the target still determines the score
paragraphs: Cont-COMET retains COMET’s source–hypothesis–reference structure. Each stream is encoded with surrounding sentences, but the final sentence representation is pooled only over tokens belonging to the current sentence. A subtle choice matters: the translation hypothesis is surrounded by reference context, rather than context generated by the translation system. Otherwise, errors in neighboring machine translations could contaminate the evidence used to judge the target.

Selection combines semantic relevance with locality. Reference sentences receive a cosine-similarity score multiplied by a distance-decay factor. The metric selects high-scoring sentences, restores their original document order, and respects the encoder’s 512-token limit. Preceding and following sentences are both eligible. Context-aware fine-tuning then uses WMT2020 ratings aligned with document information; WMT2021 and WMT2022 provide the held-out evaluation. The interactive example isolates selection, with illustrative similarities rather than encoder outputs.

evidence.title: System-level gains can hide worse sentence judgments
paragraphs: The most revealing comparison is not simply Cont-COMET against COMET. On WMT22, adding three preceding and three following sentences only at inference raises system-level Pearson correlation from 0.910 to 0.952, but lowers segment-level Kendall correlation from 0.349 to 0.292. The trained six-sentence Cont-COMET setting reaches 0.943 and 0.354 respectively. Context-only inference can therefore improve how entire systems are ranked while making individual sentence judgments less faithful to human ratings.

Selection itself is a smaller contribution: the WMT22 ablation changes system correlation from 0.942 without selection to 0.943 with it, and segment correlation from 0.353 to 0.354. The stronger lesson is to train under the conditions in which the metric will be used. These correlations also do not directly establish that the model detects a particular discourse error; the paper evaluates agreement with human quality judgments rather than reporting an error-type detection benchmark.

reading_notes: Re-read full method and result/ablation tables. Distinguish system Pearson from segment Kendall. Demo reproduces the selection formula on authored text and hand-set similarities; it does not run COMET or score translations.

demo.title: Which context reaches the evaluator?
demo.description: Cont-COMET scores every reference sentence in the document by cosine similarity to the current sentence, discounted by α for each sentence of distance, keeps the highest-scoring ones up to a budget, and restores document order (Section 2.2). Change the budget, the decay factor and the eligible side.
demo.note: Illustrative: the document, its cosine similarities and every α value (the paper does not report α). Adapted: the selection rule from Section 2.2. Computed: selection scores and the chosen context. As α falls, selection approaches an adjacent window of the same size; as α approaches 1, distant but similar sentences compete. No model or translation metric runs here.
